quiz.title: Seminar 04: Text Processing — Regex, GREP, SED, AWK
quiz.description: Formative quiz for assessing knowledge about text processing in shell

metadata.subject: Text Processing
learning_outcomes: LO1: Write functional BRE and ERE regular expressions
LO2: Use grep with main options for text searching
LO3: Transform text with sed (substitution, deletion, insertion)
LO4: Process structured data with awk (fields, calculations)
LO5: Combine tools in efficient pipelines

questions.question_text: Which regex metacharacter matches ANY single character (except newline)?

answers.feedback:
The dot (.) matches exactly one character, whatever it may be.
* = zero or more of the preceding
? = zero or one of the preceding
+ = one or more of the preceding
Confusion with * from shell globbing (where * = any characters)
Confusion with ? from shell globbing (where ? = one character)
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text: Which grep option displays ONLY the text that matched, not the entire line?

answers.feedback:
-o (only-matching) displays only the portion that matched.
-v = inverts selection (lines that do NOT match)
-c = counts matched lines
-l = displays only file names with matches
Confusion of -v with 'verbose' (in grep it means invert)
Confusion of -c with 'count characters' (it counts lines)
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text: In sed, which command deletes lines that match a pattern?

answers.feedback:
d = delete (deletes the line)
p = print (displays the line)
s = substitute (replaces)
q = quit (stops processing)
Confusion with 'p' which does the opposite (prints)
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text: For GNU grep, what is the MAIN difference between BRE and ERE in these examples?

answers.text: In BRE, metacharacters +, ?, {}, (), | require escaping with backslash
answers.feedback:
In BRE (Basic Regular Expressions), the characters +, ?, {}, (), | are 
literal by default and must be escaped (\+, \?, etc.) to act as GNU BRE operators.
Escaped +, ? and | are GNU extensions, not portable POSIX BRE syntax.
In ERE (Extended), these are metacharacters by default.

Example:
  grep 'ab+c' file       # BRE: searches literally for "ab+c"
  grep -E 'ab+c' file    # ERE: searches for "a" followed by 1+ "b" followed by "c"
Review the explanation.

answers.text: ERE does not support grouping with parentheses
answers.feedback: Review the explanation.

answers.text: BRE works only on Linux, ERE on all systems
answers.feedback: Review the explanation.

answers.text: Non-empty lines whose first character is not #
answers.feedback:
The first ^ = anchor for the start of line
[^#] = any character EXCEPT #
Thus: non-empty lines that start with a character different from #; empty lines do not match.

Note: ^ has two different meanings:
- Outside [] = start of line
- Inside [] at the beginning = negation
Confusion: the second ^ is not an anchor, but negation in character class
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text:
What will this command display?

echo -e "abc\nABC\nabC" | grep -i 'abc'

answers.feedback:
The -i option makes the search case-insensitive.
All three variants (abc, ABC, abC) match.
Forgetting that -i ignores case for ALL characters
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text:
What will this command display?

echo "hello world" | sed 's/o/O/'

answers.feedback:
Without the 'g' flag, sed replaces only the FIRST occurrence on each line.
To replace all occurrences: sed 's/o/O/g'
Assumption that sed replaces all occurrences by default
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text:
What will this command display for the line "ana:are:mere"?

echo "ana:are:mere" | awk -F: '{print $2}'

answers.feedback:
-F: sets the delimiter to ":"
$2 = the second field
The line is split into: $1=ana, $2=are, $3=mere
Confusion about field indexing (starts at 1, not 0)
Forgetting that -F changes the default delimiter (space)
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text: Which command extracts IPv4-shaped dotted decimal candidates from log.txt (without validating octets 0–255)?

answers.feedback:
The correct pattern:
- [0-9]{1,3} = 1-3 digits
- \\. = literal dot (escaped)
- (){3} = the group repeats 3 times
- -o = displays only matches
- -E = Extended regex (for {})

Option D is wrong because the unescaped . matches any character.
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.
The unescaped dot matches any character, not just '.'

questions.question_text: Which sed command deletes all completely empty lines (not whitespace-only lines) from a file?

answers.feedback:
^$ = pattern for empty line (start followed immediately by end)
d = delete command
/pattern/d = deletes lines that match

Option B only replaces the empty line with nothing, but the line remains.
Option C deletes lines that contain at least one character (the opposite).
Option D deletes ALL lines.
Confusion between substitution with empty string and line deletion
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text: For a non-empty, headerless comma-delimited file with numeric column 3 and no quoted fields or embedded commas, which awk command sums that column?

answers.feedback:
-F, = comma separator (CSV)
sum+=$3 = adds $3 to the variable sum (for each line)
END = block executed after processing all lines

Option D resets sum to $3 instead of adding (missing +).
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.
Difference between sum=$3 (assignment) and sum+=$3 (addition)

questions.question_text: Which pipeline counts how many unique lines contain "ERROR" in all .log files?

answers.feedback:
-h = suppress filename in output (otherwise each line has a prefix)
sort = necessary before uniq (uniq works on adjacent lines)
uniq = removes duplicates
wc -l = counts lines

Option B counts ALL occurrences, not unique lines.
Option D: uniq without sort does not work correctly.
Review the explanation.
Review the explanation.
uniq MUST be preceded by sort (works on consecutive lines)

questions.question_text:
Complete the sed command that replaces ALL occurrences of "foo" with "bar":

sed 's/foo/bar/___' file.txt

answers.feedback:
The 'g' flag (global) makes the substitution on all occurrences in the line,
not just the first.

questions.question_text:
A colleague wrote this command but it does not work as expected:

grep 'error|warning' server.log

The command finds nothing, even though the file contains lines with "error" and "warning".
What is the problem?

answers.text: Missing -E; in BRE, | is literal, not alternation
answers.feedback: Understanding the BRE vs ERE difference is essential for debugging
Review the explanation.

answers.text: Both options A and B are correct
answers.feedback:
In BRE (grep without -E), the | character is literal.
Two correct solutions:
1. grep -E 'error|warning' server.log   (uses ERE)
2. grep 'error\|warning' server.log     (escape in BRE)

Option D does not solve the problem if the text is exactly "error"/"warning".
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text: For a comma-delimited file without quoted or embedded commas, which command uses one awk process and direct field selection to print column 2?

answers.feedback:
The keyed answer uses one awk process and direct field selection:
- It parses the line only once
- It does not create additional processes
- It is optimised for field processing

Option B: cat | cut = UUOC (Useless Use of Cat) + pipe overhead
Option C uses regular-expression substitution. Runtime performance requires a representative benchmark; it is not established by this question.
UUOC (Useless Use of Cat) - cat is not needed here
sed is powerful but not ideal for simple field extraction
Review the explanation.

questions.question_text:
You need to extract all unique error messages from a 10GB log file 
and count their occurrences. Assuming the distinct-message counts fit in memory, which approach accumulates counts before sorting only the distinct results?

answers.feedback: grep|sort|uniq works but requires sorting the entire filtered output

answers.text: awk '/ERROR/ {errors[$0]++} END {for(e in errors) print errors[e], e}' huge.log | sort -rn
answers.feedback:
awk processes the file in a single pass, storing counts in memory.
The grep|sort|uniq pipeline requires multiple passes and disk I/O for sorting.
The memory requirement grows with the number and length of distinct messages.
This structure does not establish a universal runtime advantage.

Option A works but sort on 10GB is expensive.
Option C has useless cat overhead.
Option D is equivalent to A with sed instead of grep.

answers.text: cat huge.log | grep 'ERROR' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
answers.feedback: Useless use of cat adds overhead and obscures data flow
sed -n '/pattern/p' is functionally identical to grep 'pattern'

questions.question_text:
A colleague wrote this pipeline to anonymise email addresses in logs:

sed 's/[a-z]*@[a-z]*\.[a-z]*/[REDACTED]/g' access.log

What is the PRIMARY issue with this approach?

answers.text: The regex is too greedy and will match too much text
answers.feedback: The character classes omit valid address characters; greediness is a different property

answers.text: The regex is too restrictive (misses uppercase, numbers, dots in local part)
answers.feedback:
The pattern [a-z]* only matches lowercase letters. Real email addresses contain:
- Uppercase: John.Doe@Company.COM
- Numbers: user123@domain.com  
- Dots and special chars: first.last+tag@sub.domain.co.uk

A better pattern would be:
sed -E 's/[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}/[REDACTED]/g'

The limiting issue is the character class and permitted structure, not lack of greediness.
Both patterns are simplified heuristics; they do not guarantee complete anonymisation.
Option C is incorrect; /g works correctly.
Option D is incorrect; the replacement string syntax is valid.

answers.text: sed cannot do global replacement with the /g flag
answers.feedback: The /g flag exists and works correctly in sed

answers.text: The [REDACTED] string should be quoted differently
answers.feedback: Square brackets in replacement string are valid literal characters

questions.question_text:
Construct a SINGLE pipeline command that:
1. Extracts all IP addresses from access.log
2. Counts how many times each IP appears
3. Shows the TOP 5 IPs by frequency (most frequent first)
4. Formats output as: "COUNT IP_ADDRESS"

Write your complete command below:

rubric.criterion: Correct IP extraction with grep -oE and valid regex

rubric.note: uniq only works on adjacent lines

sample_solutions:
grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
